content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) established the Vessel Sanitation Program (VSP) in 1975 in response to significant disease outbreaks on cruise ships. This program was created as a collaborative effort with the cruise ship industry to assist in the development and implementation of comprehensive sanitation programs aimed at protecting the health of passengers and crew. The VSP promotes cooperation between government and industry to identify and mitigate health risks associated with cruise ships, ensuring a clean and healthy environment onboard. Cruise ships with foreign itineraries carrying 13 or more passengers are subject to biannual inspections and, if necessary, re-inspections by VSP personnel. The program is entirely funded by user fees. Additionally, the VSP provides construction plan reviews for new builds and major retrofits, as well as on-site construction reviews when deemed necessary. Shipbuilders are responsible for covering the costs of VSP staff travel to shipyards for these reviews. The primary goal of the VSP is to establish consistent standards for the sanitary design, construction, and inspection of cruise ships. The CDC emphasizes the importance of adhering to these guidelines to maintain high public health standards onboard. The guidelines cover various ship facilities related to public health, such as food service and water systems. While shipowners and operators have the flexibility to choose equipment that meets their needs, they must ensure that the equipment complies with VSP inspection criteria and is maintained over time. The CDC encourages innovation in shipbuilding and allows for the review of new technologies, concepts, or methods upon request. The VSP evaluates such proposals and provides written feedback on their functional merits. These construction guidelines apply to ships with keels laid after February 1, 1997, and to major retrofits planned after this date. However, they do not apply to minor retrofits. The guidelines also address the design and maintenance of food service areas, water treatment systems, plumbing, waste management systems, and recreational facilities like pools and spas. Surfaces in food contact areas must be smooth, durable, and easily cleanable. Non-food contact surfaces should also be durable and resistant to corrosion. Floor materials must be non-skid and non-absorbent. Hand-washing facilities must be constructed of stainless steel and provide hot and cold running water from a single mixing faucet. These facilities should include soap dispensers, paper towel dispensers, and corrosion-resistant waste receptacles. Hand-washing sinks should be easily accessible, and permanent signs indicating the requirement for hand washing must be installed. Toilet facilities should be located near work areas, including galleys and food service areas, and must be well-ventilated. Self-closing doors and easily cleanable surfaces are required. Child care facilities must include child-sized toilets and hand-washing stations, as well as separate facilities for child care workers. Diaper-changing tables should be non-absorbent and easy to clean, with adjacent hand-washing sinks. Equipment mounting and placement guidelines require that permanently installed equipment be sealed to bulkheads or adjacent equipment to allow for easy cleaning. Equipment not sealed must have sufficient spacing to ensure accessibility for cleaning. All equipment must be constructed to prevent gaps, crevices, and sharp edges. Fasteners used in food contact areas must be corrosion-resistant and designed to prevent gaps or seams. Gaskets for refrigerators, steamers, and other equipment must be smooth, non-absorbent, and easily removable for cleaning. Drain lines for equipment must be designed for easy cleaning and maintenance, with air breaks or air gaps to prevent contamination. The CDC recognizes the evolving nature of the shipbuilding and cruise industries and periodically reviews these guidelines to ensure they remain relevant and effective. Collaboration with industry experts is encouraged to address innovations and necessary updates to the guidelines.
